title: C482/11/2015 of Avnish Kumar Vs State Of Uttarakhand AND OTHERS

paras.text:
IN THE HIGH COURT OF UTTARAKHAND AT
NAINITAL
Criminal Misc. Application No. 11 of 2015
(Under Section 482 Cr.P.C.)
Avnish Kumar ................ Applicant

versus
State of Uttarakhand and others .......... Respondents
Mr. Nagesh Aggarwal, Advocate for the applicant.
Ms. Geeta Parihar, Brief Holder for the State.
Mr. Mohd. Alauddin, Advocate for respondent nos. 2 to 9, 11 and 13.
U.C. Dhyani, J. (Oral)
The applicant is the complainant, who
set the criminal law into motion by lodging an FIR
under Sections 302, 427, 356 IPC against the
named accused (private respondents herein).
2. The trial commenced against the
accused persons. The prosecution adduced all its
evidence, but for the medical officers, who
conducted the postmortem on the dead body of
the victim and medically examined the injured
persons. Deceased and the injured were the
relatives of the complainant (applicant herein).
3. When the prosecution witnesses were
examined, the medical officers did not turn up
before the trial Court for evidence. The sessions
trial is pending since 2007.
4. There was a direction from this Court
that the trial shall be expedited. Despite affording

many opportunities, the medical officers could not
be produced before the trial court and, therefore,
the learned Additional Sessions Judge, Laksar
closed the opportunity of evidence and fixed the
sessions trial for recording the statement of the
accused under Section 313 Cr.P.C., vide order
dated 10.12.2014.
5. Aggrieved against the same, present
application under Section 482 Cr.P.C. has been
filed by the complainant.
6. Learned counsel for the applicant
submitted that a cross-case is also pending
adjudication before the trial court.
7. Learned counsel for the applicant placed
reliance upon a decision of Honíble Apex Court in
Shailendra Kumar v. State of Bihar (2002)1
SCC 655, wherein it was observed that:
ì9. In our view, in a murder trial it is sordid
and repulsive matter that without informing the
police station officer-in-charge, the matters are
proceeded by the court and by the APP and tried
to be disposed of as if the prosecution has not
led any evidence. From the facts stated above, it
appears that the accused wants to frustrate the
prosecution by unjustified means and it appears
that by one way or the other the Additional
Sessions Judge as well as the APP have not
taken any interest in discharge of their duties. It
was the duty of the Sessions Judge to issue
summons to the investigating officer if he failed
to remain present at the time of trial of the case.
The presence of investigating officer at the time
of trial is must. It is his duty to keep the
witnesses present. If there is failure on the part

of any witness to remain present, it is the duty
of the court to take appropriate action including
issuance of bailable/non-bailable warrants as
the case may be. It should be well understood
that prosecution cannot be frustrated by such
methods and victims of the crime cannot be left
in a lurch.î
[Emphasis supplied]
8. The law, therefore, stipulates that all
out efforts should be made by the prosecution,
as well as the trial court, to procure the
attendance of material prosecution witnesses
by lawful means. The evidence of the medical
officers ought not have been closed by learned
Addl. Sessions Judge, in the instant case, only
because the sessions trial is pending since
2007 and a direction has been given by the
Honíble High Court to expedite the trial.
9. A perusal of the impugned order
indicates that the summons were issued to the
witnesses, which were not returned by the police
station concerned. The trial court ought to have
ensured that the summons were served upon the
prosecution witnesses. Thereafter, if summons
were served upon the prosecution witnesses and
they did not turned up, the bailable warrants
could have been issued. If, still, the prosecution
witnesses did not turn up after service/execution
of bailable warrants, then the non-bailable
warrant could be issued. If non-bailable warrants
are also not executed by the police station
concerned, a letter was required to be sent to the

Director General (Police) and Director General
(Medical Health), which has not been done in the
instant case.
10. The evidence of the prosecution
witnesses has been closed only because a warning
was given to the prosecution on a previous date
that the evidence would be closed, if the
prosecution witnesses do not turn up.
11. It is the submission of the learned
counsel for the applicant that out of two
witnesses, Dr. V.C. Pathak was till recently posted
in Doon Hospital, Dehradun and Dr. Richa is
posted in Sarojini Naidu Medical College, Agra.
12. Chapter VI Cr.P.C. deals with
processes to compel appearance, which
includes, appearance of the witnesses. Resort
should, therefore, be had to procure the
attendance of witnesses as per the provisions
of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 in a
proper manner.
13. Considering the facts of the case and
submissions of learned counsel for the parties,
this Court is of the opinion that the order
impugned is bad in law and, therefore, is liable to
be set aside.

14. As a consequence thereof, application
under Section 482 Cr.P.C. is allowed. The
impugned order dated 10.12.2014 passed by
learned Addl. Sessions Judge, Haridwar is set
aside. Learned trial court is directed to procure
the attendance of the medical officers, in
accordance with law, and only thereafter should
proceed to decide murder-trial.
 (U.C. Dhyani, J.)
 03.05.2017
Mahinder/
